title: Each official’s sponsored measures that were lobbied for
question: Of the measures each official sponsored, how many were lobbied on, with how much lobbying spend behind them, did the lobbying circle give to the sponsor, and what did the clients receive afterwards?
finding: Across 97 lobbied measures whose clients sought passage, a sitting supervisor was a sponsor in 46 of 111 cases where the clients’ circle had given to that supervisor in the two years before introduction (41.4%) and in 293 of 977 where it had not (30.0%); shuffling the giving among the supervisors sitting for each measure gives 41.4 on average against 46 observed, within chance. 1 of 10 supervisors with enough cases show a gap beyond chance on their own (about 0.5 expected by chance). Most lobbied measures sponsored: Rafael Mandelman (84 of 2,279), Aaron Peskin (60 of 1,046), Ahsha Safai (60 of 1,140).
how: For each official: every ordinance, resolution, motion or charter amendment they sponsored since 2015 (the Board’s record), and those tied to lobbying by file number or, separately, by subject words (an inference). Fees are what the clients paid the firms in the years of contact. “Circle gave” counts measures where the lobbying clients, their officers, the lobbyists or their firms contributed to the sponsor’s committees from two years before introduction until passage, and the dollars, each contribution once. “Awards” are amounts in the measure itself where the client is its named counterparty; “City paid the clients afterwards” is the payment ledger for the three fiscal years after passage, largest figure per client. The chance test asks, measure by measure, whether supervisors the circle had given to were sponsors more often than the other supervisors then sitting; it uses only measures where clients sought passage.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. Sponsors and donors find each other because they agree: a business group gives to the supervisors who share its outlook and those supervisors write the measures it likes. A gap beyond chance therefore shows association, not cause, and an official with few lobbied measures cannot be tested at all. City payments after a measure passed are mostly unrelated to it; only the “awards” column is money the measure itself authorized. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
